strengths: The problem has an identifiable interested audience: researchers studying high-dimensional classification with strong correlations and dense covariance matrices. Sparsity after whitening offers a useful perspective alongside sparsity of the original discriminant direction.

The whitening, screening, and classification pipeline is understandable. The motivating example and discussion of FAIR, CAT-LDA, and rotation-based methods help explain its rationale and relationship to previous work.
The experimental design includes relevant baselines, independent simulated test samples, 200 Monte Carlo replications with reported standard deviations, and two gene-expression applications.
weaknesses: Required: The main proofs do not establish consistency under the advertised assumptions. Condition 3 states only λ_k = O(p), which neither guarantees diverging spikes nor the bounded spike ratios used in Appendix B.2; it permits, for example, λ_1 = p and λ_d = 1. Appendix B.4 also concludes under log(n)log(p) = o(n), stronger than the theorem's log(p) = o(n). Supply valid proofs under the stated assumptions or narrow the theorems and headline claims. These gaps affect the central correctness criterion.

Required: Several Bayes-optimality statements are incorrect or insufficiently qualified. Equation (3.1) uses −||ζ||²/2 where the Gaussian error formula requires −||ζ||/2. Section 5.1 incorrectly treats Fisher LDA as generally Bayes optimal for common elliptical distributions with unequal priors: sub-Gaussian tails do not make their likelihood ratios linear. Restrict this extension appropriately or change its optimality target. Also explicitly justify the training-proportion convergence used in (B.42); bounded n_1/n_2 alone does not imply convergence to the test prior odds.

Required: The simulation results contain a substantial, independently checkable inconsistency. For Model 2, the stated means and covariance give squared Mahalanobis distance 10(1+9ρ)/[(1−ρ)(1+19ρ)]. At ρ = 0.9, the Bayes error is approximately 0.0196%, whereas Table 5 reports an oracle error of 5.40%. This discrepancy is far beyond Monte Carlo variability. Table 2 also repeats several results exactly between ρ = 0.7 and 0.8. Audit the data generation, oracle implementation, and tables, and provide corrected results before drawing comparative conclusions.

Required: Adaptivity claims exceed the supplied analysis. Section 2.3 promises consistent estimation of both d and s, but no consistency result for estimating d is provided. The experimental 90% explained-variance rule is not generally rank-consistent: in Model 1 with ρ = 0.5, the single population spike explains only approximately half the variance. Furthermore, the support-recovery analysis assumes fixed bounded sparsity and a minimum signal strength and studies hard thresholding, rather than the cross-validated procedure used experimentally. Clearly separate these guarantees and narrow the abstract's apparent growing-sparsity claim.

Required: Resolve the eigenvalue convention in the whitening estimator. Section 2.3 defines Λ̂ as the largest sample covariance eigenvalues, which already include the noise contribution, but then defines D̂ = (Λ̂ + σ̂²I)^−1/2. Clarify whether this is intentional additional regularization or a notation error, and align the estimator, appendix algebra, and experimental implementation.

Required clarification: The model-size comparisons count coordinates in different representations. A selected whitened coordinate generally depends on every original variable through the dense whitening matrix. Thus, the 12 PCLDA coordinates in Table 9 do not establish selection of only 12 genes. Although Section 2.2 acknowledges the distinction between supports, the empirical conclusions should consistently distinguish transformed dimension from original-variable sparsity.

Optional: After resolving the correctness issues, repeated real-data splits, inclusion of CAT-LDA in the real-data comparisons, and sensitivity analyses for rank selection and covariance misspecification would strengthen the practical conclusions.
